t: Corruption and judicial reform in Latin America
abs: This paper examines the nature and pace of judicial reforms in Latin America. Part I describes, in general terms, the current state of the courts throughout the region. The economic analysis presented in this section explains the impact of the judiciary on democracy and economic development. Part II analyses how factors related to corruption within the courts combine to increase the political institutional inertia observed during judicial reforms. This part takes into account both the expected costs and expected benefits of judicial reform, as perceived by government officials in general and judges in particular. Part II also addresses the proliferation of corruption in terms of the expected costs and benefits of engaging in corrupt activities.

t: The changing face of low pay in Britain
abs: Pay may be considered to be ‘low’ if it is not a fair reward for work done, or if it does not provide an adequate means of subsistence. The first of these approaches implies that policy should be concerned with individual employees and their wage rates. The second suggests that the adequacy of wages should be examined in the context of total household income. This study considers both perspectives and introduces a method of combining them into a single analytical framework. For the purposes of this analysis we choose to define low pay as a gross hourly wage below two thirds of the median for all employees. On this basis, we find that around one in five employees in Great Britain was low paid in 1994–95. As expected, of these the majority were young single people or married women. However, the number of men in the 25–49 age group who were low‐paid had risen significantly since the late 1960s, while the number of low‐paid employees aged 16 or 17 dropped very dramatically over the period. Female employees were more than twice as likely as male employees to be low paid in 1994–95, but they were six times as likely as men to be low paid at the end of the 1960s. Considering pay as a means of subsistence, we find that around 13% of low‐paid employees in 1994–95 were living in household poverty, up from 3–4% at the end of the 1960s. Other than for lone parents, the benefits system is shown to have a very limited role in lifting low‐paid employees out of household poverty.

t: Cross‐cultural perspectives: Toward an integrated theory of elder abuse
abs: Due to the use of unrepresentative samples, the absence of general agreement on the definition of elder abuse, and a general lack of theoretical integration, the prolific knowledge we have of the concept of elder abuse tells us little about the prevalence or about cultural differences in the social context, construction, and individual expression of elder abuse. This paper will argue that current conceptions of elder abuse originate with health and social services professionals in Canada and North American, who export their ‘authoritative knowledge’ to health and social service professionals in other countries and societies. The cross‐cultural anthropological literature will be used to describe several possible approaches to developing a definition of elder abuse that will be conceptually useful and methodologically relevant in a variety of cultural settings or contexts. Beyond the problems involved in definition we will consider the questions and issues that must be addressed in developing an integrative theoretical framework within which to interpret elder abuse.

t: Domestic energy conservation in a cold climate
abs: In 1992 the British Government made a commitment at the Rio Conference to reduce CO2 emissions to the levels recorded for 1990 by the year 2000. This represents about a 6% cut of around 15 million tonnes a year. This objective is unlikely to be met. Currently, about 28% of CO2 emissions come from households and a very significant reduction in CO2 could be achieved if the energy efficiency of dwellings was improved. This article will show that the odds have been consistently set against the prospect of a planned deployment of energy saving measures under the current administration and considers the prospects of improvement under a Labour Government. This article reveals the resistance to change by the status driven consumer behaviour of Britain's householder and the profit orientation that blinds industry to ecological crisis. The lack of government's action to promote energy saving measures, or provide funds to achieve its stated aims in the reduction of CO2 is predicated upon the inter‐relationship between consumer behaviour and industrial lobbying. The analysis will show that ‘policy initiatives’ are halfhearted at best and serve to promote only the ‘image’ of an administration which is concerned for the environment. The arguments that follow are based on a sociological analysis of the transformation of domestic consumption in the twentieth century and proceeds from the view that it is not possible to reverse expectations on the comfort, leisure, facility and functionality of the household. In this context it assesses the prospects for change under a new administration.

t: Family obligations and social policy: The case of child support
abs: The UK Child Support legislation has been very controversial. This article considers whether this reflects mainly problems with implementation or whether there are more fundamental problems with the principle that separated parents are always, and in all circumstances, financially liable for the support of their children. Comparisons with Australia highlight particular problems with the way the policy was put into practice in Britain. But it is here argued that changing employment and family patterns create other problems for this legislation, much more difficult to resolve. The article also places child support in the wider context of the way in which social policies define and enforce particular definitions of family obligations and explores what this might tell us about the nature of the relationship between attitudes, behaviour and policy.

t: Towards a learning society — Definition and measurement
abs: This article focusses on the fashionable concept of the learning society. It outlines the origins of the idea of a learning society; underscoring the different definitions of the concept that have resulted from two strands of thought ‐ economists and training experts, who have advanced the economic imperative for a more highly educated and skilled national workforce, and educationalists, who have often sought to construct a broader social and political case for an increased emphasis upon learning. The article then goes on to provide a working definition of a learning society; and probes what societal characteristics, infrastructures, expectations, behavioural norms and cultural values would support such a society. An attempt is made to identify criteria that might aid measurement and judgement on the progress of any nation towards the status of a learning society, and the contribution which economics might make to this project is reviewed as an example of the issues and difficulties that will need to be resolved before a comprehensive set of aids to measurement and judgement can be fully developed. Having defined what characteristics a learning society might be expected to possess, and outlined some means of establishing the degree to which a society has moved towards acquiring these, the article then offers a brief preliminary review of British progress against two sets of indicators — social class, and the importance of skills within the British labour market.

t: UK immigration policy: ‘Firm but fair’, and failing?
abs: This paper investigates the effectiveness of the UK immigration policy. For over two decades UK immigration policy has had clearly stated aims; to limit immigration for permanent settlement to a minimum, subject to the needs of the labour market and to obligations to dependents, genuine refugees and other exceptions. Government sources routinely describe it as firm but fair’. ‘Primary immigration’ is claimed, both by the Home Office and by the Commission for Racial Equality and by immigrant organizations, almost to have ended. The phrasing of the UK immigration policy incorporates certain ‘escape clauses’. Nonetheless if it is intended to reduce, or at least to prevent the increase of immigration defined demographically, then it has not been dramatically successful since its inception and has clearly been failing in that purpose since the mid‐1980s. This is partly because of the increase in asylum claiming since that time, and the failure to remove rejected claimants with no entitlement to remain in the UK. Although outside the ‘immigration policy’ in the strict sense, the 1993 legislation which was intended to curb asylum claiming has demonstrable not succeeded. The more general failure primarily concerns immigrants from the New Commonwealth, most of whom have entered the UK since the imposition of controls, and asylum claimants from the New Commonwealth and from the rest of the Third World.

t: Eastward enlargement of the EU — EU strategy and future challenges
abs: This paper assesses the prospects for eastward enlargement of the EU and the challenges that enlargement poses both to the applicant countries and to the EU and existing member states. The paper analyzes the EU's pre‐accession strategy and the institutional and policy issues facing the EU in proceeding successfully with eastward enlargement While the EU's pre‐accession strategy does represent a substantial commitment to eventual accession of the central and east European applicant countries, the overall approach is technocratic and ad hoc. The lack of a clear strategic outlook reflects in part uncertainty about the future direction of the EU and the impact that other major policy developments, notably the single currency, will have. It also reflects lack of agreement among EU member states about the future development of the EU and differing commitments to the process of enlargement. While the criteria and timetable for accession are not precise, substantially more progress has been made with the pre‐accession framework than with institutional and policy change. An EU of 27 member states will have to address seriously the question of differentiated integration or flexibility. Flexibility is a topic at the 1996 intergovernmental conference but since the first accessions are unlikely to occur before 2002 at the earliest, major institutional decisions at this stage are unlikely. Serious discussion of policy reform is itself on hold until after the IGC. The twin dangers of a relatively slow eastward enlargement are firstly that EU institutional structures may develop in an ad hoc and inadequate way and secondly that it could undermine — or at least not support — the political and economic transition processes in some of the central and east European countries.

t: Transforming urban infrastructure provision—The emerging logic of demand side management
abs: The provision of electricity, water and transportation forms a vital underpinning to urban development. Despite this importance, the mode by which infrastructure services are provided has been largely taken for granted and has attracted relatively little interest from urban studies and policy‐ making communities. This paper, based on the results of an 18 month ESRC Global Environmental Change programme project, reconnects urban policy to infrastructure management by highlighting how the adoption of supply‐led or more demand‐responsive modes of infrastructure provision critically shapes the intensity, and so the relative environmental impact, of networked services in contemporary cities. The paper highlights how DSM initiatives create a ‘new context’ within which infrastructure providers and users form a shared interest in the tailoring of supply and demand providing a powerful impetus to energy and water efficiency measures and more integrated transport packages. The paper argues that local policy makers must forge new coalitions of interest with infrastructure providers in order to reconnect urban policy to more environmentally sensitive forms of network management.

t: Community and contracts: Tensions and dilemmas in the voluntary sector response to HIV and AIDS
abs: Voluntary action rooted in community activism was central to the earliest collective responses to AIDS in Britain and the US, and resulted in the emergence of a wide range of community and non‐governmental organisations working to alleviate the impact of the epidemic on affected communities. Drawing on data from a series of in‐depth case studies conducted among voluntary agencies working in the field of HIV and AIDS in Britain, this paper illuminates some of the tensions and contradictions facing such agencies as they seek to respond to changes in Government policy. Central among the themes to emerge are tensions over service norms and the role of volunteers, between self‐help and altruism, informal versus formal organisational structure, political campaigning and service delivery, responding to national or to local needs, generalism and specialism, and autonomy and co‐ordination. Future challenges identified include targeting and mainstreaming, as well as maintaining intact the political project that stimulated the emergence of many organisations.

t: Towards a deconstruction of ‘environment’ in the regeneration of the Thames Gateway
abs: This paper is intended as a contribution to the debate surrounding ‘appropriate devebpment'for the Thames Gateway. In particular, it explores, through qualitative analysis of the Development Plans of its constituent planning authorities, the extent to which ‘environment’ guides regeneration initiatives in the Gateway. The paper initially provides a chronology of the Gateway Initiative from the Government's concept of regeneration of what was then designated the East Thames Corridor, through the consultation process to the Thames Gateway Planning Framework. Through an exploration of ‘environment’ as an analytical concept the paper identifies the problematic in the assertion of the Thames Gateway Planning Framework that the goals of environmental improvement are self‐evident. It argues that since there are multiple perceptions of ‘environment’ which are historically, culturally and contextually specific, policies and strategies for environmental improvement and/or protection will be unlikely to trigger common understandings or common responses. Through an analysis of community responses to the Thames Gateway Consultation Document and local and regional authority Development Plans, the paper highlights conflicts between community perceptions of environmental quality and planners visions for ‘environmental improvement’ in the Thames Gateway region. The paper concludes by arguing that failure to fully incorporate community perceptions of “valued environments’ and to secure full community participation in setting the agenda for environmental improvement in the Thames Gateway regeneration process, will ultimately undermine its sustainable and enduring environmental, economic and social vitality.

This article reviews changes in the demography of the family in Britain. It considers the decline infertility, waning marriage and remarriage, the increase in cohabitation, trends in divorce, out‐of‐wedlock births and the emergence of new family forms including lone parent families and step families. It then considers whether the UK has a family policy—concluding that we do not have the government machinery for such a policy and that governments have not sought to influence behaviour in respect of fertility, female labour supply, marriage, cohabitation and lone parenthood. In fact, despite some of their rhetoric the present Government has had a rather laissezfaire attitude to family change. The unprecedented increase in poverty among families with children is reviewed and the case for a policy to tackle at least this element of family change is made. Two policies are singled out as crucially important to families—policies for full employment and policies that enable lone mothers to work.

t: Ten turbulent years—The effects on the bus industry of deregulation and privatisation
abs: The report of the Transport Select Committee (1995) into the consequences of bus deregulation brought together a substantial body of evidence and opinion about the present state of the bus industry in Great Britain. Working from the basis of this information, it is possible to reflect upon what has happened since the Transport Act 1985 which de‐regulated the bus industry came into effect, to compare the consequences with the predicted outcomes and to consider whether further legislative or policy change is needed to secure different outcomes to those which have so far emerged.

t: Research and policy: What determines the relationship?
abs: The relationship between research and policy is a matter of much current interest to policy makers in health. This paper uses historical approaches and case studies to examine the nature of the interrelationship. Drug policy (the evaluation of methadone maintenance in the 1970s and of needle exchange in the 1980s) and alcohol policy (the changing fortunes of the Ledermann hypothesis relating total alcohol consumption to population based harm) provide examples of how the relationship operates. Research can provide the legitimation for particular policy alliances; the role of medical civil servants and medical experts in the UK has historically played a crucial gatekeeping’ role.

t: Eco‐labelling and environmental policy: Policy confusion persists
abs: The EU Eco‐label scheme was originally devised as a piece of consumer protection legislation, designed to standardise product environmental performance claims. The label is the first EU policy instrument to focus upon product design, with previous measures concentrating on pollution abatement technologies. The scheme is designed to identify the best products available, based on a series of Life Cycle Analysis‐derived criteria. However, after six years of product group studies, only one label has been awarded. The process has become beset with difficulties. These problems, and some alternative approaches are discussed. This form of intervention has received international and internal EU opposition on the grounds that it constitutes an artificial trade barrier. As an isolated, voluntary code, the scheme is an inefficient piece of environmental regulation, and can only become relevant if its operation is reformed as part of a co‐ordinated set of environmental objectives, which include consumer information.

t: The low‐skill low‐pay problem: Lessons from Germany for Britain and the US
abs: Over the last 20 years in both the US and Britain, the situation of unskilled workers has worsened relative to the rest of the workforce. In both countries, the poor, if not getting poorer are at least not improving their lot. In Germany, however, they are getting richer: workers in the bottom decile of the male earnings distribution in Germany earn twice as much as their counterparts in the US, where real wages for the low paid have been falling since the 1980s (the position of low paid workers in Britain falling somewhere between these two.) Given that the unemployment rate of the unskilled in Germany is much the same as in the US and lower than in Britain, this paper asks what lessons might be drawn from the German experience by policy‐makers in Britain. The paper considers both long‐term ways of raising the pay of those at the bottom end of the UK or US earnings distribution through the education system, and shorter term approaches through direct demand expansion or tax cuts /job subsidies. Accepting the desirability of a focus on the provision of work, the paper argues that a combination of minimum wages and job subsidies could be effective in providing reasonably paid jobs for the unskilled.

t: Financial dependency on men: Have women born in 1958 broken free?
abs: This paper examines some evidence from the 1958 NCDS birth cohort about what is actually happening to financial imbalance within British couples. The increased proportion of women in the labour force is not uniformly matched by an equivalent increase in the share of women's earnings in the household budget. While women approach half of the labour force, few women in couples of this, or other, generations bring home as much as half the total cash. A minority have successfully combined a continuous full‐time career with purchased childcare and an equal contribution to the couple's cash, but many more still leave the labour market on motherhood and return to part‐time jobs. They remain, at least partially, financially dependent on pooling income with their partners, and, eventually, on derived benefits such as widows’ pensions. Dual career couples are matched by another minority, where neither has a job, the woman is doubly dependent on the man's state benefits, and arguably trapped by them into further dependence. Policies to enhance women's earning power need to be complemented by policies which support the interest in joint resources of whichever partner contributes more unpaid labour. Cohabiting women appear almost as vulnerable should their partnership break down as married

t: Custody in the police station: How do England and Wales measure up in Europe?
abs: The Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 introduced a new system of safeguards governing police powers and procedures in England and Wales. Though it was the subject of vociferous criticism at the time, and critics continue to scrutinise its limitations, the Act is now widely accepted as representing a significant step forward in relation to the rights of people detained in police stations. What is less well known is how domestic practices compare with the situation in other countries. Based on evidence collected by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment, this article compares the treatment of people in custody in police stations in England with the situation in other parts of Europe.
